# Lecture 16.1: Kolmogorov's Extension Theorem (I)

## Construction of Finite Independent Families

::: {#def-iid-sequence}
Let $(S, \mathcal{B})$ be a measurable space and let $X_n : (\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P) \to (S, \mathcal{B})$, $n \in \mathbb{N}$, be measurable maps defined on a **common** probability space $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)$, with laws (pushforward measures) $\mu_{X_n} \triangleq P \circ X_n^{-1}$. The sequence $\{X_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ is **independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.)** if:

1. **Independence.** $\{X_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ is independent in the sense of @def-indep-rvs; explicitly, for every **finite** subfamily $X_{n_1}, \dots, X_{n_k}$ with $n_1 < \dots < n_k$ and all $B_1, \dots, B_k \in \mathcal{B}$,
$$
P\Bigl( \bigcap_{i=1}^k \{ X_{n_i} \in B_i \} \Bigr) = \prod_{i=1}^k P(X_{n_i} \in B_i).
$$
2. **Identical distribution.** There is a single probability measure $\mu$ on $(S, \mathcal{B})$ with $\mu_{X_n} = \mu$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Independence of an infinite family is thus a condition on finite subfamilies only. Unless stated otherwise we take $(S, \mathcal{B}) = (\mathbb{R}^d, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d))$; nothing in the definition requires this choice.
:::

To construct finite collections of independent random variables with prescribed probability laws $\mu_1, \dots, \mu_N$, we use product probability spaces. Since @cor-product-measure-existence constructs only the two-factor product, we first record the $N$-fold construction, which also requires identifying the $N$-fold product $\sigma$-algebra of @def-product-sigma-algebra (defined directly by $N$-fold rectangles) with an iterated two-factor product.

::: {#prp-finite-product-measure}
## Existence and Uniqueness of Finite Product Measures

Let $(S_1, \mathcal{B}_1, \mu_1), \dots, (S_N, \mathcal{B}_N, \mu_N)$ be $\sigma$-finite measure spaces with $N \ge 2$, and set $S \triangleq \prod_{n=1}^N S_n$. Then, under the canonical bijection $S \cong \bigl( \prod_{n=1}^{N-1} S_n \bigr) \times S_N$,
$$
\bigotimes_{n=1}^N \mathcal{B}_n = \Bigl( \bigotimes_{n=1}^{N-1} \mathcal{B}_n \Bigr) \otimes \mathcal{B}_N ,
$$ {#eq-product-sigma-associativity}
and there exists a **unique** measure $\bigotimes_{n=1}^N \mu_n$ on $\bigl( S, \bigotimes_{n=1}^N \mathcal{B}_n \bigr)$ satisfying
$$
\Bigl( \bigotimes_{n=1}^N \mu_n \Bigr)(B_1 \times \dots \times B_N) = \prod_{n=1}^N \mu_n(B_n) \quad \forall\, B_n \in \mathcal{B}_n .
$$ {#eq-n-fold-rectangle-formula}
This measure is $\sigma$-finite, and it is a probability measure whenever every $\mu_n$ is.
:::

::: {.proof}
## Proof of @prp-finite-product-measure

**Associativity of the product $\sigma$-algebra (@eq-product-sigma-associativity).** Write $\mathcal{C} \triangleq \bigl( \bigotimes_{n=1}^{N-1} \mathcal{B}_n \bigr) \otimes \mathcal{B}_N$.

*($\subseteq$)* Every $N$-fold rectangle satisfies $B_1 \times \dots \times B_N = (B_1 \times \dots \times B_{N-1}) \times B_N$, a two-factor rectangle whose first side lies in $\bigotimes_{n=1}^{N-1} \mathcal{B}_n$. Hence all $N$-fold rectangles lie in $\mathcal{C}$, and since $\bigotimes_{n=1}^N \mathcal{B}_n$ is generated by these rectangles (@def-product-sigma-algebra), $\bigotimes_{n=1}^N \mathcal{B}_n \subseteq \mathcal{C}$.

*($\supseteq$)* By @lem-canonical-projections-measurable each coordinate projection $\pi_n : S \to S_n$ is $\bigotimes_{n=1}^N \mathcal{B}_n$-measurable, so by @lem-product-measurability the map $\pi_{1:N-1} \triangleq (\pi_1, \dots, \pi_{N-1}) : S \to \prod_{n=1}^{N-1} S_n$ is $\bigotimes_{n=1}^N \mathcal{B}_n \,/\, \bigotimes_{n=1}^{N-1} \mathcal{B}_n$-measurable. Under the canonical bijection $S \cong \bigl( \prod_{n=1}^{N-1} S_n \bigr) \times S_N$ the two coordinate projections of the *two-factor* product are exactly $\pi_{1:N-1}$ and $\pi_N$, so @lem-product-sigma-algebra applied with $d = 2$ gives
$$
\mathcal{C} = \sigma\bigl( \{ \pi_{1:N-1}^{-1}(A) \mid A \in \textstyle\bigotimes_{n=1}^{N-1} \mathcal{B}_n \} \cup \{ \pi_N^{-1}(B_N) \mid B_N \in \mathcal{B}_N \} \bigr).
$$
Each generator lies in $\bigotimes_{n=1}^N \mathcal{B}_n$: the sets $\pi_{1:N-1}^{-1}(A)$ by the measurability of $\pi_{1:N-1}$ just established, and the sets $\pi_N^{-1}(B_N)$ by @lem-canonical-projections-measurable. Hence $\mathcal{C} \subseteq \bigotimes_{n=1}^N \mathcal{B}_n$.

**Existence.** Induct on $N$. For $N = 2$ the assertion is @cor-product-measure-existence, which also shows that the product of two $\sigma$-finite measures is $\sigma$-finite. For $N > 2$, let $\nu \triangleq \bigotimes_{n=1}^{N-1} \mu_n$ be the ($\sigma$-finite) measure supplied by the induction hypothesis and define
$$
\bigotimes_{n=1}^N \mu_n \triangleq \nu \otimes \mu_N ,
$$
which is a measure on $\bigl( \bigotimes_{n=1}^{N-1} \mathcal{B}_n \bigr) \otimes \mathcal{B}_N = \bigotimes_{n=1}^N \mathcal{B}_n$ by @eq-product-sigma-associativity, and is $\sigma$-finite by @cor-product-measure-existence. On rectangles,
$$
(\nu \otimes \mu_N)(B_1 \times \dots \times B_N) = \nu(B_1 \times \dots \times B_{N-1}) \, \mu_N(B_N) = \prod_{n=1}^N \mu_n(B_n),
$$
using the induction hypothesis. If every $\mu_n$ is a probability measure, then taking $B_n = S_n$ gives $\bigl( \bigotimes_n \mu_n \bigr)(S) = \prod_n \mu_n(S_n) = 1$.

**Uniqueness.** The collection $\mathcal{R} \triangleq \bigl\{ \prod_{n=1}^N B_n \mid B_n \in \mathcal{B}_n \bigr\}$ is a $\pi$-system, since $\prod_n B_n \cap \prod_n B_n' = \prod_n (B_n \cap B_n')$, and $\sigma(\mathcal{R}) = \bigotimes_{n=1}^N \mathcal{B}_n$ by @def-product-sigma-algebra. By $\sigma$-finiteness choose, for each $n$, an **increasing** sequence $A^{(n)}_m \nearrow S_n$ with $\mu_n(A^{(n)}_m) < \infty$ (replace a given countable cover by the unions of its initial segments, which still have finite measure by finite subadditivity). Put
$$
R_m \triangleq \prod_{n=1}^N A^{(n)}_m \in \mathcal{R} .
$$
Then $R_m \nearrow S$ and **any** measure $\kappa$ on $\bigotimes_{n=1}^N\mathcal{B}_n$ satisfying @eq-n-fold-rectangle-formula has $\kappa(R_m) = \prod_n \mu_n(A^{(n)}_m) < \infty$. Thus $\mathcal{R}$ contains an increasing sequence of sets exhausting $S$ that has finite measure under every such $\kappa$. Consequently, if $\kappa$ and $\kappa'$ both satisfy @eq-n-fold-rectangle-formula then they agree on $\mathcal{R}$ and, exactly as in the uniqueness step of @cor-product-measure-existence (Dynkin's $\pi$-$\lambda$ theorem applied to the $\lambda$-system $\{E \mid \kappa(E \cap R_m) = \kappa'(E \cap R_m)\}$ for each fixed $m$, followed by continuity from below as $m \to \infty$), $\kappa = \kappa'$ on $\sigma(\mathcal{R}) = \bigotimes_{n=1}^N\mathcal{B}_n$. Taking $\kappa = \bigotimes_n \mu_n$ also shows this measure is $\sigma$-finite. In the probability case, where $S \in \mathcal{R}$ has measure $1$, the conclusion is also immediate from @lem-pi-system-uniqueness.
:::

Suppose you want random variables $X_1,\ldots,X_N$ such that

- $X_n$ has a particular distribution $\mu_n$, and
- $X_1,\ldots,X_N$ are independent.

The following lemma says that there is a completely canonical way to do this.

::: {#lem-finite-product-construction}
Let $(S_1, \mathcal{B}_1), \dots, (S_N, \mathcal{B}_N)$ be measurable spaces and $\mu_1, \dots, \mu_N$ be probability measures on them. Define the product space:
$$
\Omega \triangleq \prod_{n=1}^N S_n, \quad \mathcal{F} \triangleq \bigotimes_{n=1}^N \mathcal{B}_n, \quad P \triangleq \bigotimes_{n=1}^N \mu_n
$$ {#eq-finite-product-space-def}
where $P$ is the product measure of @prp-finite-product-measure. Then $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)$ is a probability space, and the canonical projections
$$
X_n(\omega) \triangleq \pi_n(\omega) = x_n, \qquad \omega = (x_1, \dots, x_N) \in \Omega,
$$
are independent random variables with marginal laws $\mu_{X_n} = \mu_n$ for $n = 1, \dots, N$.
:::

::: {.proof}
## Proof of @lem-finite-product-construction

**Probability space.** By @prp-finite-product-measure the product measure $P$ exists, is unique, and satisfies $P(\Omega) = \prod_{n=1}^N \mu_n(S_n) = 1$, so $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)$ is a probability space and the maps $X_n$ below are genuine random variables.

**Measurability.** Each projection $X_n = \pi_n : \Omega \to S_n$ is $(\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{B}_n)$-measurable by @lem-canonical-projections-measurable applied to the product $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{F} = \bigotimes_{n=1}^N \mathcal{B}_n$.

**Joint distribution on rectangles.** For any $B_n \in \mathcal{B}_n$, the simultaneous event is the product rectangle:
$$
\{X_1 \in B_1, \dots, X_N \in B_N\} = \bigcap_{n=1}^N \pi_n^{-1}(B_n) = B_1 \times \dots \times B_N.
$$
Applying $P = \bigotimes_{n=1}^N \mu_n$ and using the defining property @eq-n-fold-rectangle-formula of the product measure on rectangles:
$$
\begin{aligned}
P(X_1 \in B_1, \dots, X_N \in B_N) &= \left(\bigotimes_{n=1}^N \mu_n\right)\!(B_1 \times \dots \times B_N) \\
&= \prod_{n=1}^N \mu_n(B_n).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-product-prob-eval}

**Marginal laws.** Fix $n \in \{1,\dots,N\}$ and $B_n \in \mathcal{B}_n$. Setting $B_j = S_j$ for all $j \neq n$ in @eq-product-prob-eval, and using $\mu_j(S_j) = 1$ (since each $\mu_j$ is a probability measure):
$$
P(X_n \in B_n) = \mu_n(B_n) \cdot \prod_{j \neq n} \mu_j(S_j) = \mu_n(B_n) \cdot \prod_{j \neq n} 1 = \mu_n(B_n).
$$
Hence $\mu_{X_n} = \mu_n$.

**Independence.** Substituting $P(X_n \in B_n) = \mu_n(B_n)$ into @eq-product-prob-eval gives:
$$
P(X_1 \in B_1, \dots, X_N \in B_N) = \prod_{n=1}^N P(X_n \in B_n) \quad \forall\, B_n \in \mathcal{B}_n.
$$
For any sub-family $J \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}$ and $B_j \in \mathcal{B}_j$ ($j \in J$), set $B_j = S_j$ for $j \notin J$; then $\prod_{j \notin J} P(X_j \in S_j) = 1$, giving $P\bigl(\bigcap_{j \in J}\{X_j \in B_j\}\bigr) = \prod_{j \in J} P(X_j \in B_j)$. This reduction is needed because @def-indep-rvs demands the product rule for *every* finite subfamily, not merely for the full family. Since it holds for all non-empty $J$ and all $B_j \in \mathcal{B}_j$, the random variables $X_1, \dots, X_N$ are independent by @def-indep-rvs.
:::

---

:::{#exm-coin-toss}
## Repeated coin tosses
Suppose we want to construct three independent coin tosses, where the probability of heads is $p$. For each toss, let
$$ 
S_n=\{H,T\}, \qquad \mathcal B_n=2^{S_n}, 
$$
and define the probability measure $\mu_n(\{H\})=p$ and $\mu_n(\{T\})=1-p$. The lemma tells us to construct
$$ 
\Omega = \{H,T\}\times\{H,T\}\times\{H,T\}. 
$$
Thus, an outcome is something like $\omega=(H,T,H)$. Define the coordinate random variables
$$ 
X_1(\omega)=\omega_1,\qquad X_2(\omega)=\omega_2,\qquad X_3(\omega)=\omega_3. 
$$
So, for example, $X_1(H,T,H)=H$, $X_2(H,T,H)=T$, and $X_3(H,T,H)=H$. The probability measure is $P=\mu_1\otimes\mu_2\otimes\mu_3$. Now consider the outcome $\{X_1=H,X_2=T,X_3=H\}$. This is exactly the singleton $\{(H,T,H)\}$. Therefore,
$$ 
P(X_1=H,X_2=T,X_3=H) = p(1-p)p. 
$$
In other words, $P(H,T,H)=p^2(1-p)$. The product measure automatically gives us the multiplication rule for independent experiments.
:::

:::{#exm-different-distributions}
## Example with different distributions
Suppose we want three independent random variables: $X_1\sim N(0,1)$, $X_2\sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)$, and $X_3\sim \operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)$. Take
$$ 
S_1=\mathbb R,\qquad S_2=\{0,1\},\qquad S_3=[0,1], 
$$
and
$$ 
\Omega=\mathbb R\times\{0,1\}\times[0,1]. 
$$
Then define $X_1(x_1,x_2,x_3)=x_1$, $X_2(x_1,x_2,x_3)=x_2$, and $X_3(x_1,x_2,x_3)=x_3$. The product measure
$$
P = N(0,1) \otimes \operatorname{Bernoulli}(p) \otimes \operatorname{Uniform}(0,1) 
$$
guarantees that $X_1$, $X_2$, and $X_3$ are independent and have exactly the desired marginal distributions. Thus, the lemma is not merely about coin tosses. It provides a general construction principle:

Choose the marginal distributions$\implies$take their product measure$\implies$the coordinate variables are independent.
:::

::: {#exm-standard-normal-vectors}
## Construction of Standard Normal Vectors

To construct $d$ i.i.d. $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ random variables on $\mathbb{R}^d$, let $\gamma(x) = (2\pi)^{-1/2} e^{-x^2/2}$ be the standard Gaussian density with respect to Lebesgue measure $\lambda$ on $(\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))$, and define $d\mu = \gamma \, d\lambda$. The Gaussian integral $\int_{\mathbb{R}} \gamma \, d\lambda = 1$ is what makes $\mu$ a *probability* measure, which is required below.

Since $\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d) = \bigotimes_{j=1}^d \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})$ (the Borel $\sigma$-algebra identity of Lecture 14.2), the space $(\mathbb{R}^d, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d))$ carries the product measure $P = \mu^{\otimes d}$ of @prp-finite-product-measure. By @lem-finite-product-construction the coordinate projections $X_n(x_1, \dots, x_d) = x_n$ are i.i.d. with common law $\mu = \mathcal{N}(0,1)$; no computation of a joint density is needed for this conclusion.

The joint density is a *consequence*, not the reason. Define
$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x_1, \dots, x_d) &\triangleq \prod_{j=1}^d \gamma(x_j) \\
&= (2\pi)^{-d/2} \exp\left( -\frac{1}{2} \sum_{j=1}^d x_j^2 \right) \\
&= (2\pi)^{-d/2} e^{-\frac{1}{2}\|x\|^2},
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-multivariate-normal-density}
a non-negative Borel function on $\mathbb{R}^d$.

**The two candidate reference measures agree.** Let $\lambda^{\otimes d}$ be the $d$-fold product of one-dimensional Lebesgue measure on $\bigotimes_{j=1}^d \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})$, which exists by @prp-finite-product-measure since $\lambda$ is $\sigma$-finite, and let $\lambda^d$ denote Lebesgue measure on $\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)$. The two $\sigma$-algebras coincide by the Borel identity. Let
$$
\mathcal{R}_{\square} \triangleq \Bigl\{ \textstyle\prod_{j=1}^d (a_j, b_j] \;\Big|\; -\infty \le a_j \le b_j \le +\infty \Bigr\},
$$
with the convention $(a, +\infty] \triangleq (a, +\infty)$, and where $a_j = b_j$ is allowed so that $\emptyset \in \mathcal{R}_{\square}$. Then $\mathcal{R}_{\square}$ is a $\pi$-system, because $\prod_j(a_j,b_j] \cap \prod_j(a_j',b_j'] = \prod_j (a_j \vee a_j', \, b_j \wedge b_j']$ (interpreting an interval with left endpoint $\ge$ right endpoint as empty), and $\sigma(\mathcal{R}_{\square}) = \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)$. Both $\lambda^{\otimes d}$ and $\lambda^d$ assign the value $\prod_{j=1}^d (b_j - a_j)$ to such a box — for $\lambda^{\otimes d}$ by @eq-n-fold-rectangle-formula, for $\lambda^d$ by its defining property. Since $R_m \triangleq (-m, m]^d \in \mathcal{R}_{\square}$ increases to $\mathbb{R}^d$ with $\lambda^{\otimes d}(R_m) = (2m)^d < \infty$, the uniqueness argument of @cor-product-measure-existence (an increasing sequence of finite-measure sets **inside** the $\pi$-system) gives
$$
\lambda^{\otimes d} = \lambda^d \quad\text{on } \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d).
$$

**Computing the law.** For any box $R = \prod_{j=1}^d (a_j, b_j] \in \mathcal{R}_{\square}$ we have the tensor factorization $f \cdot \mathbf{1}_R = \bigotimes_{j=1}^d \bigl( \gamma \cdot \mathbf{1}_{(a_j,b_j]} \bigr)$. Applying @thm-tonelli to the two-factor splitting $\lambda^{\otimes d} = \lambda^{\otimes (d-1)} \otimes \lambda$ supplied by @eq-product-sigma-associativity — legitimate because $f \mathbf{1}_R \ge 0$ is Borel and all factors are $\sigma$-finite — and iterating $d - 1$ times,
$$
\int_R f \, d\lambda^{\otimes d} = \prod_{j=1}^d \int_{(a_j, b_j]} \gamma \, d\lambda = \prod_{j=1}^d \mu\bigl((a_j, b_j]\bigr) = \mu^{\otimes d}(R),
$$
the last step by @eq-n-fold-rectangle-formula. Taking $R = \mathbb{R}^d$ shows $\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} f \, d\lambda^{\otimes d} = 1$, so $\nu(E) \triangleq \int_E f \, d\lambda^{\otimes d}$ defines a *probability* measure on $\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)$. Since $\nu$ and $\mu^{\otimes d}$ are probability measures agreeing on the $\pi$-system $\mathcal{R}_{\square}$ with $\sigma(\mathcal{R}_{\square}) = \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)$, @lem-pi-system-uniqueness yields
$$
d\mu^{\otimes d} = f \, d\lambda^{\otimes d} = f \, d\lambda^d ,
$$
i.e. the law of $(X_1, \dots, X_d)$ is the standard multivariate normal distribution $\mathcal{N}(0, I_d)$.
:::


---

## Compact Infinite Product Spaces

To construct infinite sequences of random variables, we extend finite product measure spaces to infinite products. Let $Q \triangleq [0, 1]^\mathbb{N} =\prod_{n=1}^\infty [0, 1] = \{ (x_n)_{n=1}^\infty \mid x_n \in [0, 1] \}$ and let $p_n : Q \to [0,1]$, $p_n(x) = x_n$, denote the coordinate maps. We equip $Q$ with the **product topology**, i.e. the initial (coarsest) topology making every $p_n$ continuous; a base is given by the finite cylinders
$$
\bigcap_{i=1}^k p_{n_i}^{-1}(U_i), \qquad k \in \mathbb{N},\ n_1 < \dots < n_k,\ U_i \subseteq [0,1] \text{ open}.
$$ {#eq-product-topology-base}

The product topology is *not* defined by a convergence criterion; the following lemma shows that on $Q$ it is nevertheless metrizable, so that sequences do determine the topology. This is used twice below: to pass from sequential compactness to compactness in @thm-tychonoff, and to identify $\mathcal{B}(Q)$ in @lem-borel-cylinder-identity.

::: {#lem-product-topology-metric}
## Metrizability of $Q$

The product topology on $Q = [0,1]^\mathbb{N}$ is induced by the metric
$$
\rho(x, y) \triangleq \sum_{n=1}^\infty 2^{-n} |x_n - y_n| ,
$$ {#eq-product-metric-definition}
and $\rho$-convergence is exactly coordinatewise (pointwise) convergence:
$$
\begin{aligned}
&x^m = (x_n^m)_{n=1}^\infty \to x = (x_n)_{n=1}^\infty \text{ in } Q \\
&\iff x_n^m \to x_n \text{ in } [0, 1] \quad \forall n \in \mathbb{N}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-pointwise-convergence}
In particular $Q$ is a separable metric space, and compactness, sequential compactness, closedness and sequential closedness in $Q$ agree.
:::

::: {.proof}
## Proof of @lem-product-topology-metric

The series in @eq-product-metric-definition converges (terms bounded by $2^{-n}$), and $\rho$ is clearly a metric: symmetry and the triangle inequality are inherited termwise, and $\rho(x,y) = 0$ forces $x_n = y_n$ for every $n$.

*$\rho$-convergence $\Rightarrow$ coordinatewise.* Fix $n$; then $|x_n^m - x_n| \le 2^n \rho(x^m, x)$.

*Coordinatewise $\Rightarrow$ $\rho$-convergence.* Given $\epsilon > 0$, pick $N$ with $\sum_{n > N} 2^{-n} < \epsilon/2$; the remaining finitely many terms satisfy $\sum_{n \le N} 2^{-n}|x_n^m - x_n| < \epsilon/2$ for $m$ large. (This is where $\sum_n 2^{-n} < \infty$ is essential: the tail is uniformly small, which is why no analogue holds for uncountable products.)

*$\rho$ induces the product topology.* Each $p_n$ is $1$-Lipschitz up to the factor $2^n$, hence $\rho$-continuous, so the product topology is coarser than the $\rho$-topology. Conversely, given $x \in Q$ and $\epsilon > 0$, choose $N$ with $\sum_{n > N} 2^{-n} < \epsilon/2$; the basic cylinder $\bigcap_{n \le N} p_n^{-1}\bigl( (x_n - \epsilon/4, x_n + \epsilon/4) \cap [0,1] \bigr)$ is a product-open neighbourhood of $x$ contained in the $\rho$-ball $B_\rho(x, \epsilon)$. Hence the two topologies coincide.

The final assertions are the standard facts that in a metric space compactness and sequential compactness are equivalent, and that closed sets are exactly the sequentially closed sets. Separability follows since finitely supported rational sequences are $\rho$-dense.
:::

::: {#thm-tychonoff}
## Sequential Compactness of $[0, 1]^\mathbb{N}$

Every sequence $x^{(1)},x^{(2)},\ldots\in Q$ has a subsequence $x^{(m_k)}$ and some $x\in Q$ such that $x^{(m_k)}\to x$ coordinatewise, i.e.,
$$
x_n^{(m_k)}\to x_n \qquad\text{for every }n\in\mathbb N.
$$
That is, $Q = [0,1]^\mathbb{N}$ is **sequentially compact**; by @lem-product-topology-metric it is therefore also **compact**.
:::

::: {.proof}
## Proof of @thm-tychonoff
*(Cantor's Diagonal Argument)*

Let $(x^{(m)})_{m \ge 1}$ be an arbitrary sequence in $Q$.

**Step 1: Construct nested convergent subsequences.** Apply the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem (every bounded sequence in $\mathbb{R}$ has a convergent subsequence) inductively:

* **Base case ($j = 1$):** $(x_1^{(m)})_{m \ge 1} \subseteq [0,1]$ is bounded. By Bolzano-Weierstrass, extract a subsequence $m^{(1)}(k)$ such that $x_1^{(m^{(1)}(k))} \to x_1 \in [0,1]$ as $k \to \infty$.
* **Inductive step ($j \ge 2$):** Given the subsequence $m^{(j-1)}$, apply Bolzano-Weierstrass to $(x_j^{(m^{(j-1)}(k))})_{k \ge 1} \subseteq [0,1]$ to extract a **further** subsequence $m^{(j)}(k)$ of $m^{(j-1)}(k)$ such that $x_j^{(m^{(j)}(k))} \to x_j \in [0,1]$ as $k \to \infty$.

The limits lie in $[0,1]$ because $[0,1]$ is closed. (This recursive extraction uses the axiom of dependent choice; we shall not comment on such uses again.)

This yields nested subsequences $m^{(1)}, m^{(2)}, \ldots$ — each $m^{(j)}$ a subsequence of $m^{(j-1)}$ — satisfying:
$$
x_j^{(m^{(j)}(k))} \to x_j \in [0,1] \quad \text{as } k \to \infty, \quad \forall j \ge 1.
$$

**Step 2: Define the diagonal sequence.** Set $d_k \triangleq m^{(k)}(k)$ — the $k$-th element of the $k$-th subsequence. This is strictly increasing: since $m^{(k+1)}$ is a subsequence of $m^{(k)}$, write $m^{(k+1)}(j) = m^{(k)}(\sigma_k(j))$ for a strictly increasing function $\sigma_k$ satisfying $\sigma_k(j) \ge j$. Then:
$$
d_{k+1} = m^{(k+1)}(k+1) = m^{(k)}\!\left(\sigma_k(k+1)\right) \ge m^{(k)}(k+1) > m^{(k)}(k) = d_k.
$$

**Step 3: Coordinatewise convergence.** Fix any $n \in \mathbb{N}$. For every $k \ge n$, $m^{(k)}$ is a subsequence of $m^{(n)}$ (by transitivity of nesting: $m^{(k)} \subset m^{(k-1)} \subset \cdots \subset m^{(n)}$). Hence $d_k = m^{(k)}(k) = m^{(n)}(l_k)$ for a *unique* index $l_k$, since $m^{(n)}$ is strictly increasing, hence injective. Moreover $l_k$ is strictly increasing in $k \ge n$: if $l_{k+1} \le l_k$ then $d_{k+1} = m^{(n)}(l_{k+1}) \le m^{(n)}(l_k) = d_k$, contradicting Step 2. Therefore $l_k \to \infty$, and $(x_n^{(d_k)})_{k \ge n}$ is a subsequence of the convergent sequence $(x_n^{(m^{(n)}(l))})_{l \ge 1}$:
$$
x_n^{(d_k)} = x_n^{(m^{(n)}(l_k))} \xrightarrow{\;k \to \infty\;} x_n.
$$
The finitely many terms with $k < n$ do not affect the limit. Since $n \in \mathbb{N}$ was arbitrary, $x^{(d_k)} \to x = (x_n)_{n \ge 1} \in Q$ coordinatewise.
:::

::: {#cor-finite-intersection-property}
## Countable Finite Intersection Property

If $\{K_m\}_{m=1}^\infty$ is a sequence of closed subsets of $Q$ such that $\bigcap_{i=1}^m K_i \neq \emptyset$ for all $m \in \mathbb{N}$, then $\bigcap_{i=1}^\infty K_i \neq \emptyset$.
:::

::: {.proof}
## Proof of @cor-finite-intersection-property

(Each $K_m$ is automatically non-empty, by the hypothesis with $m$ in place of the index.) For each $m \in \mathbb{N}$, choose $x^m \in \bigcap_{i=1}^m K_i$. By @thm-tychonoff there are indices $m_1 < m_2 < \cdots$ and $x \in Q$ with $x^{m_l} \to x$ in $Q$.

Fix $i \in \mathbb{N}$. Since $m_l \to \infty$, choose $l_0$ with $m_{l_0} \ge i$. For every $l \ge l_0$ we have $m_l \ge m_{l_0} \ge i$, hence
$$
x^{m_l} \in \bigcap_{j=1}^{m_l} K_j \subseteq K_i .
$$
Thus $x$ is the limit of a sequence lying in $K_i$, and $K_i$ is closed, hence sequentially closed by @lem-product-topology-metric; therefore $x \in K_i$. As $i \in \mathbb{N}$ was arbitrary, $x \in \bigcap_{i=1}^\infty K_i$.
:::

---

## Kolmogorov Extension Theorem on $[0, 1]^\mathbb{N}$

The Kolmogorov Extension Theorem provides a method to construct infinite sequences of random variables with prescribed finite-dimensional distributions.

::: {.callout-note}
## Notation from here on
From this point onward, and throughout Lecture 16.2, $p_n : Q \to [0,1]$ denotes the **$n$-th coordinate** map, $p_n(x) = x_n$, and
$$
\pi_n : Q \to [0,1]^n, \qquad \pi_n(x) = (x_1, \dots, x_n),
$$
denotes the projection onto the **first $n$ coordinates**. This supersedes the earlier use of $\pi_n$ in this lecture for the $n$-th coordinate projection of a finite product $\prod_{k=1}^N S_k$.
:::

Before stating the theorem we must know that the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of the *topological* space $Q$ coincides with the $\sigma$-algebra generated by the cylinder sets, on which the theorem prescribes $P$. This is exactly what makes the uniqueness assertion meaningful; it uses that the product is **countable** and each factor is second countable, and it fails for uncountable products, where the cylinder $\sigma$-algebra is strictly smaller than the Borel $\sigma$-algebra.

::: {#lem-borel-cylinder-identity}
## Borel Sets of $Q$ are the Cylinder Sets

For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\mathcal{B}([0,1]^n) = \bigotimes_{k=1}^n \mathcal{B}([0,1])$; in particular $B \times [0,1] \in \mathcal{B}([0,1]^{n+1})$ whenever $B \in \mathcal{B}([0,1]^n)$. Moreover
$$
\mathcal{B}(Q) = \sigma\bigl( p_n : n \in \mathbb{N} \bigr) = \sigma\Bigl( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty \pi_n^{-1}\bigl( \mathcal{B}([0,1]^n) \bigr) \Bigr) ,
$$ {#eq-borel-cylinder-identity}
and the collection $\mathcal{A} \triangleq \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty \pi_n^{-1}\bigl( \mathcal{B}([0,1]^n) \bigr)$ is an algebra, hence in particular a $\pi$-system, generating $\mathcal{B}(Q)$.
:::

::: {.proof}
## Proof of @lem-borel-cylinder-identity

**Finite-dimensional identity.** Open boxes $\prod_{k=1}^n I_k$ with $I_k \subseteq [0,1]$ relatively open with rational endpoints form a countable base of the (second-countable, metric) space $[0,1]^n$. Every open $G \subseteq [0,1]^n$ is therefore a countable union of such boxes, each of which lies in $\bigotimes_{k=1}^n \mathcal{B}([0,1])$; hence $\mathcal{B}([0,1]^n) \subseteq \bigotimes_{k=1}^n \mathcal{B}([0,1])$. Conversely each coordinate projection $\operatorname{pr}_k : [0,1]^n \to [0,1]$ is continuous, hence Borel, so $\operatorname{pr}_k^{-1}(\mathcal{B}([0,1])) \subseteq \mathcal{B}([0,1]^n)$ for every $k$; since $\bigotimes_{k=1}^n \mathcal{B}([0,1]) = \sigma(\operatorname{pr}_1, \dots, \operatorname{pr}_n)$ by @lem-product-sigma-algebra, the reverse inclusion follows. Combining this with the associativity identity @eq-product-sigma-associativity gives $\mathcal{B}([0,1]^{n+1}) = \mathcal{B}([0,1]^n) \otimes \mathcal{B}([0,1])$, so $B \times [0,1] \in \mathcal{B}([0,1]^{n+1})$ for $B \in \mathcal{B}([0,1]^n)$.

**$\supseteq$ in @eq-borel-cylinder-identity.** Each $p_n$ is continuous for the product topology, hence Borel measurable, so $\sigma(p_n : n \in \mathbb{N}) \subseteq \mathcal{B}(Q)$. Furthermore $\pi_n = (p_1, \dots, p_n)$ has all components $\sigma(p_1, \dots, p_n)$-measurable, so by @lem-product-measurability it is $\sigma(p_1, \dots, p_n) \,/\, \bigotimes_{k=1}^n \mathcal{B}([0,1])$-measurable; by the finite-dimensional identity this means $\pi_n^{-1}(\mathcal{B}([0,1]^n)) \subseteq \sigma(p_1, \dots, p_n)$. Hence the second and third $\sigma$-algebras in @eq-borel-cylinder-identity coincide, and both are contained in $\mathcal{B}(Q)$.

**$\subseteq$ in @eq-borel-cylinder-identity.** By @lem-product-topology-metric the metric $\rho$ of @eq-product-metric-definition induces the product topology. Let $\mathcal{U}$ be the countable collection of finite cylinders $\bigcap_{k \le N} p_k^{-1}(I_k)$ with $N \in \mathbb{N}$ and each $I_k \subseteq [0,1]$ relatively open with rational endpoints. The argument in the proof of @lem-product-topology-metric shows that for every $x \in Q$ and $\epsilon > 0$ there is a member of $\mathcal{U}$ containing $x$ and contained in $B_\rho(x, \epsilon)$ (choose $N$ with $\sum_{n > N} 2^{-n} < \epsilon/2$ and rational-endpoint intervals of length $< \epsilon/2$ around $x_1, \dots, x_N$). Hence $\mathcal{U}$ is a countable base, so every open $G \subseteq Q$ is a countable union of members of $\mathcal{U}$, and each member of $\mathcal{U}$ lies in $\sigma(p_n : n \in \mathbb{N})$. Therefore $G \in \sigma(p_n : n \in \mathbb{N})$ and $\mathcal{B}(Q) \subseteq \sigma(p_n : n \in \mathbb{N})$. (Countability of $\mathcal{U}$ is exactly what fails for uncountable products.)

**$\mathcal{A}$ is an algebra.** $Q = \pi_1^{-1}([0,1]) \in \mathcal{A}$; complements are handled within a fixed level since $Q \setminus \pi_n^{-1}(B) = \pi_n^{-1}([0,1]^n \setminus B)$; and two cylinders of orders $m \le n$ can be brought to the common order $n$ via $\pi_m^{-1}(B) = \pi_n^{-1}(B \times [0,1]^{n-m})$, after which unions are taken inside $\mathcal{B}([0,1]^n)$. Finally $\sigma(\mathcal{A}) = \sigma(p_n : n \in \mathbb{N}) = \mathcal{B}(Q)$.
:::

::: {#thm-kolmogorov-extension-unit-interval}
## Kolmogorov Extension Theorem (Compact Base Space)

For each $n \in \mathbb{N}$, let $\nu_n$ be a probability measure on $([0, 1]^n, \mathcal{B}([0, 1]^n))$. Suppose the sequence $\{\nu_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ satisfies the **projective consistency condition**:
$$
\nu_{n+1}(B \times [0, 1]) = \nu_n(B) \quad \forall B \in \mathcal{B}([0, 1]^n), \, \forall n \in \mathbb{N}
$$ {#eq-kolmogorov-consistency-cond}
which is meaningful by @lem-borel-cylinder-identity. Then there exists a unique probability measure $P$ on $(Q, \mathcal{B}(Q))$ such that
$$
P\bigl( \pi_n^{-1}(B) \bigr) = \nu_n(B) \quad \forall B \in \mathcal{B}([0, 1]^n), \, \forall n \in \mathbb{N},
$$ {#eq-kolmogorov-target-measure}
equivalently $P \circ \pi_n^{-1} = \nu_n$ for every $n$; that is, $\{\nu_n\}$ is exactly the family of finite-dimensional distributions of $P$.
:::

Three comments on the statement.

* **Notation.** In @eq-kolmogorov-target-measure the cylinder $\pi_n^{-1}(B)$ is often written $B \times Q$, using the canonical homeomorphism $Q \cong [0,1]^n \times [0,1]^{\{n+1, n+2, \dots\}}$. Strictly, $B \times Q$ is not a subset of $Q$, and we use $\pi_n^{-1}(B)$ throughout.

* **Uniqueness.** Uniqueness is immediate from @lem-borel-cylinder-identity and @lem-pi-system-uniqueness: @eq-kolmogorov-target-measure determines $P$ on the $\pi$-system $\mathcal{A}$, and $\sigma(\mathcal{A}) = \mathcal{B}(Q)$. Existence is the substantive assertion.

* **Scope of the consistency condition.** @eq-kolmogorov-consistency-cond only requires consistency under deletion of the *last* coordinate. For a family indexed by the initial segments $\{1, \dots, n\}$ this is enough: iterating it gives $\nu_m\bigl( B \times [0,1]^{m-n} \bigr) = \nu_n(B)$ for all $m > n$. For families indexed by arbitrary finite subsets $F$ of a general index set $T$, the condition must be strengthened to include *permutation* consistency, $\nu_{\sigma F} = \nu_F \circ \sigma^{-1}$, in addition to marginal consistency.

Finally, the hypothesis that the base space is the **compact** interval $[0,1]$ is not a technical convenience: the theorem is false for general measurable state spaces. The proof converts finite additivity on the cylinder algebra $\mathcal{A}$ into countable additivity by an inner-regularity argument, using @thm-finite-borel-radon (in the form @cor-radon-on-borel-subset, which applies to the cubes $[0,1]^n$) together with @cor-finite-intersection-property. The proof is given in Lecture 16.2; the case of $\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}$ is then obtained by transporting the problem to $(0,1)^\mathbb{N} \subseteq Q$ along a homeomorphism $\mathbb{R} \cong (0,1)$.

:::{#exm-consistency-condition}
Let $\lambda$ denote the uniform probability measure on $[0,1]$. For each $n$, define 
$\nu_n=\lambda^{\otimes n}$ the $n$-fold product measure on $([0,1]^n,\mathcal B([0,1]^n))$. Thus, $\nu_n$ is the joint distribution of $n$ independent $U[0,1]$ random variables. We want to check that
$$ 
\nu_{n+1}(B\times[0,1])=\nu_n(B) 
$$
for every $B\in\mathcal B([0,1]^n)$.

Suppose $B=B_1\times\cdots\times B_n$, where each $B_j\in\mathcal B([0,1])$. Then
$$ 
B\times[0,1] = B_1\times\cdots\times B_n\times[0,1]. 
$$
Because $\nu_{n+1}=\lambda^{\otimes(n+1)}$, we have
$$ 
\begin{aligned} 
\nu_{n+1}(B\times[0,1]) &= \lambda(B_1)\cdots\lambda(B_n)\lambda([0,1])\\ 
&= \lambda(B_1)\cdots\lambda(B_n), 
\end{aligned} 
$$
because $\lambda([0,1])=1$. But $\nu_n(B) = \lambda(B_1)\cdots\lambda(B_n)$. Therefore,
$$
\nu_{n+1}(B\times[0,1]) = \nu_n(B). 
$$

Suppose $\nu_2=\lambda\otimes\lambda$ describes the joint distribution of $(X_1,X_2)$
and $\nu_3=\lambda\otimes\lambda\otimes\lambda$ describes the joint distribution of $(X_1,X_2,X_3)$. Take, for example, $B=[0,0.3]\times[0.5,0.8]$. Then
$$ 
B\times[0,1] = [0,0.3]\times[0.5,0.8]\times[0,1]. 
$$
The consistency condition says
$$ 
\nu_3\left( [0,0.3]\times[0.5,0.8]\times[0,1] \right) = \nu_2\left( [0,0.3]\times[0.5,0.8] \right). 
$$
Indeed, $(0.3)(0.3)(1)=0.09$ while $(0.3)(0.3)=0.09$. The third coordinate contributes nothing because we allow it to take any value in $[0,1]$.

Thus the family $\nu_1=\lambda$, $\nu_2=\lambda^{\otimes2}$, $\nu_3=\lambda^{\otimes3}$,$\ldots$ is projectively consistent. Kolmogorov's theorem then gives a unique probability measure $P$ on $Q=[0,1]^{\mathbb N}$ such that
$$ 
P\circ\pi_n^{-1}=\lambda^{\otimes n} \qquad\forall n. 
$$
In other words, the theorem constructs the probability law of an infinite sequence 
$(X_1,X_2,X_3,\ldots)$ of independent $U[0,1]$ random variables from its finite-dimensional distributions.

So the conceptual picture is:
$$ 
\underbrace{\nu_1,\nu_2,\nu_3,\ldots}_{\text{finite-dimensional distributions}} \quad\xrightarrow{\text{Kolmogorov Extension}}\quad \underbrace{P}_{\text{law of the infinite sequence}} 
$$
:::
